building.template2: It is late autumn, evening: the miller's house stands two storeys high built of timber frame on stone and is worn with age, there are old grey chips round the chopping block, no fresh ones, your eye catches that the ridge beam over the door is rotten at one end, its door is locked. The shutters are closed, the chimney is cold, no smoke, dead leaves drifted against the doorstep, undisturbed. You hear no sound from inside, there is a smell of woodsmoke from the other houses in the lane, none from this one. Nobody else in the lane, there is low evening sun on the west wall.

haiku.text: Two storeys of worn timber frame on stone sit in low evening sun on the west wall, and the lane's woodsmoke stops at this house. The ridge beam over the door is rotten at one end, the chimney is cold, the shutters are closed, and the door is locked, with dead leaves undisturbed against the doorstep and only old grey chips round the chopping block. No sound comes from inside, and nobody else is in the lane.

sonnet.text: Your eye goes straight to the ridge beam over the door, rotten at one end, on a worn two-storey house of timber frame on stone, and you know that's work for someone before the winter. person.template2: Midday: Gil looks hungry, thin in the face, he has mud to the knee, you see him walking slowly, favouring the arm, he is bent under a load of split timber on his back. He has come from the deep wood, there is a cut on the left forearm, bound with a rag, still seeping, you see pine resin on his hands, the split timber is pine, freshly cut. Breathing hard, you can hear, there is a smell of sweat and fresh-cut pine. He walks alone, the day is bright and mild.

haiku.text: Gil comes out of the deep wood alone at midday, thin in the face and breathing hard under a load of freshly split pine. Your eye goes to the rag bound on his left forearm, still seeping, and to the mud on his legs as he favours that arm and walks slowly past you. He smells of sweat and fresh-cut pine, and resin shows on his hands.

field.template2: Late summer, late afternoon: the barley field by the stream is sown with barley, overhead, rooks feeding on the trampled grain, the rows are choked with thistle and dock thick along the rows, the grain is half ripe, heads still green at the tips. You find a gap in the hurdle fence on the eastern edge, one hurdle down, the crop is trampled flat along the eastern edge and you read cattle hoof prints there. Cattle lowing in the pasture beyond the eastern edge, you can hear, there is a smell of dung on the trampled edge. The stream running low and clear, nobody else in the fields.

haiku.text: You stand alone in the late afternoon with the barley by the stream, half ripe and still green at the tips, and your eye goes straight to the eastern edge, where it lies trampled flat. Cattle hoof prints mark the crushed stalks, dung sits on the ground, and rooks feed on the spilled grain while cattle low in the pasture beyond a gap where one hurdle of the fence is down. Thistle and dock stand thick along the rows, and the stream runs low and clear beside it all.

land.template2: Early autumn, morning now: the wind is cold, from the north, you see a thick column of smoke rising from the next valley to the north, geese flying south, earlier than usual, the sky is clear, pale. Wind in dry beech leaves; the geese calling, you can hear, there is a smell of woodsmoke on the wind, faint. You see beech leaves already turning, you see white frost on the grass in the shade, the stream low, a herder driving cattle down from the high pasture.

haiku.text: Geese are flying south earlier than usual, their calls carried on the cold north wind through beech leaves already turning. Under a clear, pale sky, a thick column of smoke rises from the next valley to the north, and faint woodsmoke comes to you on the air. The stream runs low, white frost lies on the grass in the shade, and a herder is driving cattle down from the high pasture.

tracks.template2: Early morning: there are deer prints, fresh, heading out of the wood toward the field, every print made since the rain last night, you see fresh deer droppings by the field gate, there is one set of boot prints, large, going into the wood, none coming out in the soft mud. You find a broken hazel twig at head height where the boot prints enter. Water dripping from the branches; a woodpecker drumming deeper in the wood, you can hear, there is a smell of wet earth and leaf mould. Nobody in sight; the village below still quiet, grey dawn light, mist in the hollows.

haiku.text: Fresh deer prints, made since the rain last night, run out of the wood toward the field, and fresh droppings lie by the gate, so the deer have only just passed.
